text:
Do not pin exact versions in one shared `requirements.txt`. The two roles want opposite things. Split the dependency declaration into two files, one per role.

## Why the roles conflict

A library states what it can work with. A service states what it did work with. An exact pin in a library propagates to every team that imports you. If your library pins `requests==2.31.0` and another package pins `requests==2.32.0`, the resolver fails. The importer cannot patch a CVE in a transitive dependency without a release from you. A transitive dependency is a package your dependency pulls in, not one you name yourself.

A service has no importer. Here an exact pin is the point. It makes the build reproducible, and it makes a rollback mean something.

## The shape I recommend

1. Put the library dependencies in `pyproject.toml` as ranges. Set a lower bound on the oldest version you test. Set an upper bound on the next major version only.
2. Put the extra service dependencies in `requirements.in`. Add the line `-e .` so the service picks up the library from the same tree.
3. Generate `requirements.txt` from `requirements.in`. Use `uv pip compile requirements.in -o requirements.txt --generate-hashes`.
4. Install with `pip install -r requirements.txt` in the deploy path and in the service container.
5. Never hand-edit `requirements.txt`. The compile step overwrites it. Keep the generated header comment, because it tells the next reader to edit `requirements.in`.

Example for the library file:

```toml
[project]
dependencies = [
  "requests>=2.31,<3",
  "pydantic>=2.5,<3",
]
```

## Two things the split does not cover

Ranges hide breakage until an importer hits it. Run your library test suite twice in CI. One job installs the lock file. The other job installs the newest allowed versions with `--upgrade`. The second job catches an upstream break before your users report it.

The upper bound is a guess about the future. `<3` is safe, because a major bump is a stated break. Do not write `<2.32`. A tight upper bound blocks your importers and ages badly.

## When to break this rule

Pin the library exactly only if it is internal, and if every importer deploys on your release schedule. That is a service in a library's clothes. Say so in the README, so nobody publishes it to a wider audience later.
